intro: Introduction to European Union Law. Lecture two: the institutions, part one — the European Council and the Commission.

slides.4: The course map returns, with the institutions as the topic of this lecture.
slides.6: The advisory bodies. Article 13, paragraph 4 of the Treaty on European Union adds the Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions. They are called institutions of the Union, but with an immediate qualification: they are primarily supporting and advising, so they do not decide. In a question about who adopts an act, they never appear as the author.
slides.10: A classroom exercise: students ask a chatbot what the European Council is, and the answer is then checked against what the lecture says.
slides.18: How the European Council really works — club behaviour. The search for compromises through long-term package deals, resting on an understanding of solidarity and reciprocity, and facilitated by agreements among the chiefs without formal backing from national administrations or legislatures. A strong tendency towards informality. And the problem named is current: that shared understanding of solidarity and reciprocity is disturbed by questions about the rule of law in some member states, and by the legal action that has followed.
slides.27: The Commission: the facts. It is a collegiate body — it decides as one, not department by department. President Ursula von der Leyen, the High Representative, and one Commissioner per member state. The Secretariat General connects the political and administrative levels; under it, the administration consists of Directorates-General and services. Seat in Brussels, a five-year term, meetings not open to the public.
slides.29: Parliamentary supervision — and its limits. Parliament approves the composition, and elects the President, in quotation marks, since that election follows the European Council's proposal, which must take the election result into account. Parliament can also bring down the whole Commission by a vote of no confidence. Now the limits: no such rights exist over the European Council or the Council of the European Union, because those are composed of nationally elected politicians. And the censure motion works only against the entire Commission, never against a single Commissioner.
slides.32: The administration: the Secretariat General, and under it the Directorates-General, each headed by a Director-General and divided into directorates and units. The European civil service numbers fewer than forty thousand staff — two thirds civil servants and temporary staff, with many employed in the language services. That figure is smaller than most people assume, and it is a good corrective to talk of a Brussels bureaucracy.
slides.38: How the Commission decides. Presence quorum: fifty per cent plus one. Decision-making quorum: a simple absolute majority of the constituent members — that is, of all Commissioners, not merely of those present. In practice decisions are usually taken by consensus. Compare that with the European Council: two thirds presence, and consensus decisions.
